title: Exceptional longevity · FOXO3
summary: FOXO3 is one of the two most consistently replicated human longevity genes. The G allele at rs2802292 is enriched among centenarians across Japanese, German, and other cohorts; GG homozygotes had roughly 1.5-2.7x the odds of reaching very old age in the original studies. The effect is on probability of long survival, not a guarantee for any individual.

interpretations.GG: Two copies of the longevity-associated G allele. In studies of long-lived people, this genotype was found more often than expected — roughly 1.5-2.7x the odds of reaching exceptional old age compared with TT. This shifts probability modestly; lifestyle and chance still dominate individual lifespan.
interpretations.GT: One G copy linked to longevity gives a middle result between GG and TT on average. Studies find a smaller rise in G carriers among people who live to very old ages. This is one small chance factor among many influences on lifespan.
interpretations.TT: No copies of the longevity-associated G allele. This is a common genotype and simply lacks the modest statistical advantage seen for G carriers in longevity cohorts. Plenty of centenarians carry this genotype; the variant explains only a small slice of survival differences.

title: Longevity · APOE (e2/e3/e4)
summary: APOE is the strongest common DNA factor linked to human lifespan so far. The two sites below combine to define the e2, e3, and e4 forms. The e4 form, marked by C at rs429358, appears less often in people who reach 100. The e2 form, marked by T at rs7412, appears a little more often. Many e4 carriers still live very long lives. These are shifts in odds, not fate.

interpretations.TT: No e4-defining C allele at this position. Combined with rs7412, this genotype corresponds to the e2 or e3 forms of APOE, which are not associated with the reduced odds of reaching extreme old age seen for e4.
interpretations.CT: One C allele, which usually corresponds to one copy of APOE e4. On average, each e4 copy is associated with lower odds of surviving to extreme old age (roughly 30-50% lower odds of centenarian status in various cohorts). This is a statistical shift; many e4 carriers reach their 90s and beyond.
interpretations.CC: Two C copies usually mark APOE e4/e4, found in about 2% to 3% of people. This type is least common among people who reach very old ages. It is still only one factor. Health, habits, and chance strongly shape lifespan.
No e2-defining T allele at this position. Together with rs429358 this corresponds to the e3 or e4 forms of APOE, without the modest longevity enrichment reported for e2 carriers.
interpretations.CT: One T copy usually marks one APOE e2 copy. Studies of people who reach 100 find e2 a little more often than expected. This fits a small rise in the average odds of very long life. Habits and other genes matter much more.
interpretations.TT: Two T copies usually mark APOE e2/e2. This type is rare, at about 1 in 200 people. It follows the favorable lifespan pattern seen for e2 on average. Data on this exact type are limited because it is rare.

title: Longevity · CETP I405V
summary: In Ashkenazi Jewish families with very long lives, people with two valine copies of CETP I405V, shown as GG, appeared more often among those who reached 100. They also had larger HDL and LDL particles and lower CETP levels. Other groups have found mixed results, so this link remains tentative.

interpretations.AA: Two copies of the A (isoleucine) allele. This genotype did not show the longevity enrichment reported for VV homozygotes in the Ashkenazi study. Given mixed replication elsewhere, any true effect of this variant on lifespan is likely small.
interpretations.AG: One G valine copy and one A isoleucine copy give a middle result for the fat-particle size linked to this site. In the first study, only people with two valine copies showed a longevity rise. This is a modest, unconfirmed factor at most.
interpretations.GG: Two G copies mark the valine VV type. It was about three times more common in Ashkenazi people who reached 100 than in younger controls. This type was also linked to larger fat particles in blood. Other groups have not always found the same result, so the link is interesting but unproven.

title: Longevity · IGF1R
summary: Reduced insulin/IGF-1 signaling extends lifespan in worms, flies, and mice. In a small Italian study, the A allele of IGF1R rs2229765 was associated with lower circulating IGF-1 levels and was more frequent among long-lived people, hinting that the same pathway matters in humans. Evidence remains thin and awaits large-scale replication.

interpretations.AA: Two A copies were linked to lower average IGF-1 in blood in the first study. This type was also more common among people who lived a long time. The study group was small, so this is an early signal, not a proven effect.
interpretations.AG: One copy of the A allele. Carriers showed lower average IGF-1 levels than GG homozygotes in the original study. Any lifespan effect from this single variant is likely small and is not yet firmly established.
interpretations.GG: No copies of the A allele. This genotype was associated with somewhat higher average IGF-1 levels and was not enriched among the long-lived in the original study. IGF-1 levels are shaped by many genes plus nutrition and health status, so genotype alone says little.

citations.label: Bonafè et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2003

title: Longevity · SIRT1
summary: SIRT1 is the human match for sirtuin genes that affect lifespan in lab animals. One small Turkish study found that SIRT1 protein levels rose with age. Older people with AG at rs7895833 had the highest levels. The authors proposed a possible link to long life. No other study has confirmed this early result.

interpretations.AA: Two A copies have no proven link to human lifespan. The available studies are small and their results conflict. No sound effect for this exact type has been found.
interpretations.AG: One A and one G copy had the highest SIRT1 protein levels among older people in one small study. The authors viewed this as a possible link to long life. This is an early clue, not a result confirmed by other studies.
interpretations.GG: Two G copies have no proven link to lifespan. Current evidence is too limited for a sound claim about this type. Sirtuin research in people is still active, and larger studies may change the picture.

title: Telomere length · TERT
summary: Telomeres protect the ends of chromosomes and grow shorter with age. Their average length is partly inherited. TERT makes the main working part of telomerase, which can extend telomeres. At rs2736100, the C copy is linked to slightly longer telomeres on average. Each copy shifts length by only a fraction of a standard deviation.

interpretations.AA: Two A copies are linked to slightly shorter telomeres in white blood cells on average. This DNA effect is small beside the wide range seen in people of the same age. Habits and chance also affect measured length.
interpretations.AC: One A and one C copy give a middle telomere length on average. The C copy linked to longer telomeres is also linked to slightly higher odds of some cancers. Longer is therefore not always better. This site shows a trade-off.
interpretations.CC: Two C copies are linked to modestly longer telomeres on average. The group shift is tens to about two hundred DNA base pairs, not a separate body state. Any net effect on lifespan seems small.

title: Telomere length · TERC region
summary: The TERC gene encodes the RNA template that telomerase uses to extend telomeres. rs10936599, near TERC, is one of the strongest common-variant influences on mean telomere length: the C allele is associated with longer average telomeres and the T allele with shorter. Effects are small relative to person-to-person variation.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C allele, the most common genotype, associated with slightly longer average telomere length at this locus. Telomere length still varies widely between individuals with the same genotype.
interpretations.CT: One copy of each allele, associated with intermediate average telomere length. The per-allele shift is on the order of 75-100 base pairs — meaningful at a population level but small for any one person.
interpretations.TT: Two T copies are linked to slightly shorter telomeres on average. Shorter measured length has group-level links to some conditions that rise with age. This one DNA change explains only a small part of the difference.

title: Longevity · Klotho KL-VS
summary: Klotho is a hormone linked to aging. Mice without it age early, while mice that make extra klotho live longer. Human studies of the KL-VS change, rs9536314 or F352V, show an unusual pattern. One copy may be linked to better survival and thinking, while two may lose or reverse that effect. Other studies have found mixed results.

interpretations.GG: Two KL-VS G copies are rare, at about 2% to 3% of people. In the first study, this type appeared less often at older ages. This suggests that any benefit may apply only to people with one copy. Data for GG are sparse, so confidence is low.
interpretations.GT: One KL-VS G copy is linked in several studies to a modest survival benefit. Other work links it to slightly better memory and thinking scores on average. Some groups did not find these results, so the link remains tentative.
interpretations.TT: This common type has no KL-VS copy and serves as the comparison group in klotho studies. No harm is linked to lacking the change. It simply lacks the possible one-copy benefit, which is not yet confirmed.

citations.label: Arking et al., Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 2002

title: Survival at older ages · TP53 codon 72
summary: p53 helps guard against cancer by making damaged cells die. Stronger p53 activity may also reduce tissue repair. At codon 72, the proline form, shown here as G, has weaker cell-death activity. In a Danish study of 9,219 people, Pro/Pro was linked to about 6% higher survival over 12 years than Arg/Arg. The median survival gap was about three years. This link is still debated.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C (arginine-72) allele, the most common genotype in European populations. In the Danish study this group served as the reference and had somewhat lower 12-year survival than Pro/Pro homozygotes. The absolute difference was modest and other cohorts have reported mixed results.
interpretations.CG: One arginine and one proline copy were linked to about 3% higher survival over 12 years than Arg/Arg in the Danish study. This small group difference still needs to be confirmed in other populations.
interpretations.GG: Two G copies mark proline-72. In the Danish study, this type was linked to about 6% higher survival over 12 years and about three more years of median survival than Arg/Arg. Better survival after serious illness may help explain it. This remains a small, debated factor, not a forecast for one person.

citations.label: Ørsted et al., J Exp Med 2007
van Heemst et al., Exp Gerontol 2005

title: Inflammation and aging · IL6 -174
summary: Long-term, low-level inflammation is linked to many conditions that rise with age. Interleukin-6 is one of its main signals. The IL6 promoter change -174G/C, or rs1800795, affects IL-6 activity in some settings. One Danish study found GG a little more often at older ages. Other studies disagree on the effect and even its direction.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the -174C allele. Studies of this genotype's effect on IL-6 levels and survival disagree with one another; no consistent lifespan association has emerged. At most this is a very small factor within the broader biology of inflammation and aging.
interpretations.CG: One copy of each allele. Intermediate in most models of this promoter variant's effect on IL-6 expression. Given the contradictory literature, no confident statement about longevity can be attached to this genotype.
interpretations.GG: Two -174G copies appeared a little more often with age in one Danish group. This may point to a survival benefit. Other studies found no effect or the opposite direction, so a link to lifespan is not proven.
